soluble groups with distinct residual finiteness characteristics. Specifically, we
define two naturally occurring classes of groups with near exponential residual
finite behavior and demonstrate that these classes are distinguishable. One group
has a unique property where every finite group can be embedded within it, while
the other consists of a broader range of groups, including those that are not
directly divisible. In addition to these findings, we confirm the validity of
Polak's initial definition and provide a detailed characterization of groups
within the $\omega$-hierarchical framework. This work also yields significant
implications for the study of groups with near exponential residual finite behavior
and resolves several long-standing open questions. Notably, we demonstrate that
groups within the $\omega$-hierarchical class are inherently locally finite, while
the range of groups with near exponential residual finite behavior is significantly
broader, encompassing examples such as surface groups and certain types of
arithmetic groups. Furthermore, we establish the existence of an infinite set of
$2$-generator groups with near exponential residual finite behavior, while
concurrently proving that no such group can be a torsion group. Lastly, we
investigate the relationship between locally finite groups with near exponential
residual finite behavior and the property of being directly divisible. This study
ultimately reveals that the latter property is not inherent to all groups within
this class and poses an open question regarding the existence of non-directly
divisible locally finite groups with near exponential residual finite behavior.

The challenge of identifying long-term or steady-state solutions for kinetic models of gas flow is a complex one. Due to the high dimensionality of these models, direct numerical methods become computationally demanding, especially when rarefied gases are modeled. In this study, two-dimensional simulations of multiscale gas flow through a periodic array of cylinders at low Knudsen numbers are performed using the kinetic model based on Gallis' model for fluid motion. To accelerate the convergence of kinetic model solutions to fluid dynamics solutions, two approaches are investigated: the iterative integration of the kinetic model and the application of coarse-grid initial conditions. Both methods demonstrate rapid convergence towards the fluid dynamics solution within dozens of cycles. It is found that the kinetic energy density and its components converge at different rates. Additionally, convergence is observed in the moments of the distribution function, the flow rate, and the force exerted by the gas on the obstacle. However, the convergence of the distribution function itself is not evaluated in this study. These findings suggest that steady-state solutions for rarefied gas flow can be efficiently discovered using direct numerical methods, facilitated by the proposed techniques. Furthermore, this study provides valuable insights for the development of accelerated algorithms for discovering multiscale kinetic model solutions. Such algorithms could potentially be applied to more complex scenarios, such as flows through 3D arrays of obstacles, by utilizing parallel computing capabilities. We introduce the concept of a class-level prototype, aiming to represent an entire class with a single example. Prototypes are widely used in metric learning, typically set as global averages. However, this method may not effectively capture the essence of individual classes when encountering diverse and complex data sets. To address this issue, we propose the Coherent prototype, chosen from class-level data variations, promoting learning in data-scarce scenarios. The Coherent prototype is computed as the average of individual prototypes, generated through optimal pair assignments, balancing the intra-class and inter-class distances. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in metric learning, especially in few-sample learning, while providing a more interpretable and stable representation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the Coherent prototype in various data conditions and settings. Additionally, we propose a novel training technique, called prototype alignment, to enhance the stability of learned representations. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets, including the CUB-200-2011 bird dataset, the CAROLA cars dataset, and the Stanford Online Marketplace dataset. Moreover, we showcase the semantic representativeness of class-level prototypes in the Coherent approach. To facilitate prototype-based research, we release our code and pre-trained models at https://github.com/uta-sleek/prototype-learning. Understanding the human mind's functional brain network is a pressing scientific issue. Recent studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have attempted to address this problem, but most efforts have focused on regional connections between individual brain regions, neglecting the complexities of interactions between regions. In contrast, we propose a more comprehensive approach, where the functional brain network is defined by complete correlation between all brain regions. Our analysis, using fMRI data from the 1000 Brain Human Connectome Database, reveals a central hub consisting of 92 key nodes, forming a large-scale network with 379 edges. Notably, our findings show that this complete functional network is highly robust, retaining 90% of its edges when subjected to noise, and shares striking similarities with the anatomical brain network. Furthermore, our analysis identifies critical nodes and regions within the default mode network, visual network, and auditory network, providing novel insights into the underlying mechanisms. For instance, the prefrontal cortex emerges as a pivotal node due to its widespread connections, while the superior temporal regions are identified as crucial nodes within the auditory network. Our study provides a more complete understanding of the functional brain network, shedding light on the intricate relationships between brain regions, and highlights the importance of using a comprehensive framework to characterize the human mind's functional network. The resulting complete functional brain network offers a valuable resource for understanding neurological and psychiatric disorders, as well as facilitating the development of innovative brain-machine interfaces. The associated data and code can be found at https://github.com/zhengzimingmmap/CompleteFunctionalNetwork. This study proposes a novel method for establishing wireless connections between sensors located on the ground and above ground level, without relying on cables linking them together. Ground-level sensors are designed to capture data from both the surroundings and above-ground sensors that detect atmospheric and sky conditions. Simulations were conducted to assess the performance of this link formation algorithm under various scenarios, including different numbers of aerial sensors, sensor locations, and data transmission rates. This research offers a theoretical model for ground-and-sky sensor networking and has the potential to contribute to the development of aerial robots and other aerial-related technologies. Generating realistic cell shapes poses significant difficulties due to the intricate nature of cellular processes influencing their formation. Conventional methods based on parametric or implicit models often fall short in accurately capturing cell morphology. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new learning strategy that utilizes a two-stage process: (1) a GAN network produces a continuous function that represents the cell's surface features; (2) a differentiable solver uses the output from the GAN to generate cell shapes that conform to anatomical constraints, fine-tuned through adversarial training. Our novel approach enables the creation of high-quality synthetic cell shapes through the integration of a normalizing flow-based GAN, which preserves the topology of the data, and a numerical solver that respects the physical constraints of cell growth. As a result, we achieve state-of-the-art results in cell shape synthesis, while also introducing flexible implicit models that can be used for various downstream applications, such as visualizing cellular processes or generating development scenarios. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Analysis and experimental results are presented in a companion video. The synthetic cell shapes generated from our model can be visualized on the CellShape website. The cell shape dataset used in this research can be accessed on the CellData website. These enigmatic galaxies, often overlooked in the past, have their properties revealed for the first time using the WFC3 and NIRCam instruments. Through a combination of spectral and photometric analysis, our research provides the first comprehensive infrared-based classification system for these galaxies, based on their redshift, mass, and star formation rates. This breakthrough enables a more accurate understanding of these galaxies' evolution and their contribution to total star formation in the universe. Our research also sets the stage for future studies to explore these galaxies' complex processes, such as galaxy interactions, dust composition, and the formation of heavy elements. The fourth industrial revolution has brought about widespread adoption of cyber-physical systems (CPS) as essential components within modern manufacturing systems. These systems have introduced an element of unpredictability in scheduling due to their inherent dynamic nature. This research aims to develop an improved method for modeling the uncertainty associated with CPS-related operations in Industry 4.0 scheduling. We begin by examining the two primary sources of uncertainty in such environments: the non-deterministic uncertainty stemming from random events and the uncertainty arising from lack of information regarding specific events. Building upon the established Fuzzy Resource Constraint Scheduler (FRCs), we propose the Fuzzy Ambiguity Resource Constraint Scheduler (FARCS) to address the second source of uncertainty. FARCS achieves this by representing resource availability as subject to multiple, discrete fuzzy constraints. We illustrate the application of FARCS through a practical example and evaluate its performance using computational experiments. Results demonstrate that FARCS outperforms FRCs in most cases, while the two methods deliver identical solutions when the level of ambiguity is low. This research contributes to the development of uncertainty modeling methods for Industry 4.0 scheduling, particularly in environments characterized by non-deterministic ambiguity. This work also serves as a foundation for future research into uncertainty modeling in Industry 4.0 scheduling. We intend to extend FARCS in future studies to address the first source of uncertainty, namely non-deterministic ambiguity. Concealed Markov Models serve as a basic technique for analyzing sequential data, allowing the evaluation of probabilistic properties in the absence of detailed information about the processes generating that data. This paper presents a non-probabilistic version of CMs, referred to as Abstract Concealed Markov Models. ACMMs provide a strong way to discuss and analyze the behavioral properties of CMs without requiring any probabilistic assumptions. They are built on a simple, monadic structure that uses abstract operators to capture the key features of CMs. This framework includes methods to determine whether a given property holds for all possible behaviors of a given CM, as well as to verify if a CM's behavior satisfies a given property. ACMMs are particularly useful in contexts where detailed information about the data-generating processes is lacking, such as in data analysis or software testing. They can also serve as a foundation for developing specialized analysis tools, tailored to specific domains. For instance, we demonstrate how to use ACMMs to provide a formal verification of the observation property in the data flow analysis of a simple imperative language. Our approach has been implemented and tested using the tool L4re. Furthermore, we discuss how to extend ACMMs to handle more complex scenarios, such as CMs with multiple threads or those operating within strict time constraints. This paper examines the concept of statistical nonlocality in solid mechanics,
particularly focusing on volume-integrated stochastic fields. It is well established
that low-frequency fluctuations in material properties and external loads can yield
significant, high-frequency stochastic field components. Moreover, the memory
effects and dynamic interactions between these fields can lead to substantial
nonlocal effects. To capture these phenomena, we develop a stochastic finite
element framework based on the total Lagrangian formulation. By integrating the
stochastic Lagrangian and applying the variational principle, we derive the
stochastic equilibrium equations and compatibility conditions. Our numerical
results demonstrate that structures exhibiting both material nonlocality and
statistical nonlocality can display different behavior than structures with only
material nonlocality or no nonlocality. Specifically, we find that a plate with
material and stochastic nonlocality can deform less and experience less stress
compared to a material nonlocality structure, especially when the stochastic
amplitude is relatively high. Additionally, we find that introducing stochastic
nonlocality can alter the mode shape such that higher frequency modes are less
affected than in the material nonlocality structure. Our research aims to provide a
comprehensive understanding of the statistical nonlocality phenomenon and its
impact on engineering structures. We also hope that our work inspires further
investigation into the role of stochastic fields in modeling dynamic structures.

To achieve this goal, we formulate a problem that optimizes a weighted sum rate (WSR) metric under both power and quantization constraints. However, due to the non-convex nature and computational intensity of the resulting optimization problem, we propose an alternative solution. Building on the idea of collaborative data transmission, we reframe the problem as a single composite optimization issue, simplify it by transforming it into a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channel, and apply group least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Group LASSO) to obtain a practical solution. Experimental results confirm that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of spectral efficiency and remains close to the optimal solution. A specific type of curve known as tropical, over an algebraically closed field extended by a tropical semifield, supports a logical function semifield. This logical semifield can be represented as the composite of two semifields, one being the function field of the curve and the other being the constant semifield, viewed as a functor. The production of the logical semifield by the function field and the constant semifield depends on specific tropical moduli, which form a specific set that always remains finite. The size of the set does not exceed the 2nd embedding dimension of the tropical semifield. The work presented generalizes previous research, focusing on the case of genus zero or non-positive, and extends to any tropical curve, regardless of genus. The research also reveals that the size of the set of moduli that produces the logical semifield is bounded above by twice the 2nd embedding dimension of the tropical semifield, providing an upper limit for the first time. In a broad context, the Q-procedure has been used to make policy recommendations by incorporating a Lagrange multiplier in various types of constrained optimization problems. This paper examines how a sequence of Lagrange multipliers converges to its true counterpart as the constraint becomes increasingly accurate. This scenario is applicable in a wide range of settings, including but not limited to, dynamic programming with resource constraints. It is essential to note that the conventional notion of convergence does not necessarily apply to the Q-procedure, thus the development of novel tools such as the property of "consistent convergence." These tools enable the creation of a sequence that converges to the true Q-procedure under the condition of "consistent convergence." Furthermore, we propose and investigate a privacy preservation metric known as pragmatic privacy breach (PPB) to assess the risk. Utilizing our framework, we analyze how different privacy preservation methods impact pragmatic privacy breaches and compare them using real-world datasets. Our study contributes to the existing research in federated learning by addressing a previously unexplored aspect of privacy breaches and evaluating different preservation methods through empirical comparisons. Additionally, we highlight the significance of considering pragmatic privacy breaches in realistic federated learning settings and provide recommendations for future research. As cities become increasingly reliant on interconnected urban systems, they create value but also expose themselves to significant risks, including cyber threats. A major concern is the possibility of a massive cyber assault that cripples a city's ability to function, potentially through targeted disruption of vital services and the exploitation of vulnerabilities in urban infrastructure and devices with connected lives. To mitigate these risks, a new approach to managing resources within a city's urban infrastructure is proposed, focusing on defending against high-stakes cyber threats. A strategic game is developed to help cities respond effectively to such threats, taking into account the dynamic nature of urban networks and the rapid spread of cyber threats. Through intelligent decision-making, a city can adapt and evolve to counter these threats, protecting its most critical services and preventing widespread disruptions, even when under assault by a skilled adversary. To put this approach into practice, a comprehensive game is implemented in a simulated urban setting, incorporating real-world elements, such as the city's network topology, the functionality of its services, and the skills of its defenders and attackers. By playing out this game, cities can develop effective strategies to manage and recover from high-pressure situations, including the ability to prioritize and manage limited resources effectively, even when under assault. Our results demonstrate that this approach can be an invaluable tool for cities to prepare for and respond to severe cyber threats, offering a new perspective on the intersection of urban planning, network security, and strategic decision-making. Ultimately, this research sets the stage for a new line of investigation, exploring the intersection of urban planning, network security, and strategic decision-making through the lens of a game-theoretic framework. A user-friendly implementation of this game can serve as a valuable resource for urban planners, network administrators, and cybersecurity professionals to test their skills and strategies in a realistic and dynamic environment, potentially saving lives and reducing disruptions during severe cyber assaults. A key limitation of this work is the assumption that attackers and defenders can be clearly distinguished, warranting future research into more nuanced models of co-opetition and gray-area threats. Additionally, this game can be extended to incorporate other critical aspects of urban systems, such as social networks and urban mobility systems, offering a wealth of opportunities for further investigation. The BAG-DC method outperforms state-of-the-art retrievals in terms of performance on noisy data and demonstrates robustness across various levels of label noise. In many real-world applications of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), only a small number of node attributes or labels can be obtained due to data scarcity. This limitation hinders the potential of GNNs in uncovering hidden patterns within graphs. To address this challenge, we introduce the Insightful Pseudo-Tagging (IPT) method, a graph pre-training technique that enhances GNN performance using few-shot learning. IPT pre-trains a GNN to generate node pseudo-tags as intermediate representations, which are then refined using limited labels through pseudo-tag balancing. By doing so, IPT improves pseudo-tag quality and boosts downsteam task performance. Experimental evaluations on five public graph datasets demonstrate the superiority of IPT over existing methods in few-shot learning scenarios. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/whu-icml/Insightful-Pseudo-Tagging. IPT achieved 1st place in the Graph Deep Learning for Few-shot Learning Track of NeurIPS 2021. By leveraging Bregman proximal gradient methods, this approach can effectively estimate a parametric model representing a target probability distribution. Notably, our method's performance is characterized by strong theoretical guarantees and a clear convergence rate, supported by the properties of Bregman proximal gradient methods. When applied to simulated and real-world data, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance in comparison to established measures and other divergence-based techniques. Chain Event Networks present a compact method for modeling complex event sequences as a combination of simpler, independent events. However, the optimal breakdown of events remains unclear, with various factorization approaches proposed in the literature. We introduce a unified framework for viewing these factorizations and present a Bayesian framework for selecting the most suitable one given new data. Our approach treats the chosen factorization as a parameter and uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods to generate a posterior distribution of factorization configurations. We apply this method to the event data from the Cassini-Hyades Network and discover that multiple factorizations yield similar results, highlighting the importance of prior assumptions in modeling. This approach can be used with any CE Network model and is particularly beneficial when working with limited data. It also facilitates the creation of flat priors to determine the number of events required to model a given sequence. We provide a detailed explanation of our code for performing this analysis, which is available at https://github.com/andrewwolff/bayes-ce-nets. We conclude by suggesting that future CE Network models should include a clear statement of prior assumptions to ensure transparent and robust modeling. This transparency is crucial for validating the results of any analysis using these models. In a 2019 paper, we introduced a novel variant of the proximal point algorithm for minimizing a strongly convex and Lipschitz differentiable function, combined with a Tikhonov regularization term. This new algorithm mimics the dynamic behavior of a heavy ball in a damped inertial system, where the Tikhonov function acts as a viscous damping factor. Our original convergence analysis assumed that the Tikhonov function remains positive and bounded away from zero. However, in the present study, we relax this constraint by demonstrating that, even when the Tikhonov function approaches zero at a polynomial rate, the sequence generated by the dynamic model still converges to the minimum norm solution of the original optimization problem. Furthermore, under certain conditions, we establish that the sequence converges linearly towards the minimum norm solution, where the convergence rate is influenced by the Tikhonov function and the Lipschitz constant of the gradient. This finding is illustrated by a numerical example that highlights the importance of choosing a Tikhonov function with a suitable decay rate. The paper's findings are accompanied by a supplementary video that visually demonstrates the model's behavior. We introduce a planar graph called the SLE tetrahedron, where its edges are related to Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLE) curves. Specifically, any pair of SLE curves from the same domain share an intersection point, and when combined with their respective semantic opposites, form a closed path. This path's complement is then described as the result of merging two quantum disks via conformal gluing, where the underlying triangle of the SLE tetrahedron serves as the seed domain for the associated quantum disk process. This process is known as the conformal gluing algorithm (CGA). This construction method, the CGA, naturally generates the SLE kernel, thereby providing a solution to the Yufelevich equation and enabling the derivation of the Loewner equation's driving function. This driving function, in turn, can be used to define a family of non-intersecting SLE curves, where the curves' local times are equivalent to specific conformal welding rules. These rules govern the merging of quantum disks in triangular domains, thereby forming the SLE tetrahedron's faces. This process is analogous to the conformal loop optimization method (CLOM), where the underlying structure is a complex of triangular domains. This analogy is further explored in a companion paper, where the CLOM is applied to the SLE tetrahedron's dual, resulting in the formation of a tetrahedron of quantum triangles. Investigations into the interaction between photons and nucleon or delta resonances have been carried out using isospin symmetry. Results from on-shell and quasi-on-shell calculations, incorporating data from various experiments, indicate that an isospin-3/2, 7/2 nucleon resonance and an isospin-3/2, 7/2 delta resonance are necessary to explain observed features. This resonant structure is analogous to that of the $\Delta(3230)$ and potentially represents a new, unobserved resonance denoted as $N(7)$ or $\Delta(3230)$. This work also highlights the importance of including these resonances in models of $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction. This paper expands the existing results by incorporating two additional factors: first, it considers a broader class of typed lambda-calculi that allows for partial function applications; second, it examines the relationship between positive types, which are types free from negation, in relation to functions with non-negative arity. The research also demonstrates that regular functions corresponding to positive types cannot be represented as compositions of basic functions (Krivine embedding), and establishes that partial applications and positive types are essential in capturing the essence of typed lambda-calculi, thus resolving open questions from prior studies. Furthermore, the paper provides applications of these findings in the areas of subtyping and polymorphism. Finally, the research compares the results with respect to total functions (without partial applications) and highlights new challenges related to advanced type constructors. In this work, we modify three common models for their application in air-water mixtures to ensure they meet these thermodynamic criteria. We also introduce a novel ad-hoc correction to improve the enthalpy of vaporization in accordance with the first law of thermodynamics. Our modifications demonstrate that the phase diagram's shape and specific volumes align with those from empirical and quantum mechanical models. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive set of thermodynamic property tables that can be used for simulations in the range of 300 K to 400 K in humid air. These modifications also enable the use of the ideal gas assumption for water vapor without compromising the accuracy of the air's thermodynamic properties. In particular, this allows the enthalpy of vaporization to be represented as an increase in air's enthalpy, thereby ensuring that the total system's enthalpy remains consistent. We also present a novel expression for the water vapor's speed of sound, which is shown to be in agreement with experimental data across the specified temperature range. In addition, we examine the performance of the modified models in conjunction with finite volume method simulations to assess their accuracy. In a comparative study, we investigate the computational efficiency of the modified models and find that the corrected models require minimal adjustments to their existing code, thereby facilitating their adoption. Overall, our modifications to the models have a profound impact on their accuracy and physical coherence, which can be leveraged in a variety of applications, including computational fluid dynamics and thermodynamic property calculations. In particular, we anticipate that these modifications will be instrumental in supporting space missions that involve cryogenic systems and other high-technology endeavors. In addition to its practical applications, our work also contributes to the advancement of fundamental knowledge regarding thermodynamic models for air-water mixtures. Specifically, we demonstrate that the modified models meet all the key requirements for their accuracy, thereby ensuring their consistency with thermodynamic principles. In a broader context, our work highlights the need for a more rigorous evaluation of thermodynamic models for their application in humid air and encourages the development of models that are grounded in thermodynamic coherence. Furthermore, our work underscores the importance of computational simulations that are consistent with thermodynamic first laws and entropy production for their accuracy and physical coherence. The performance of a dialogue system heavily relies on the subsequent speech recognition step, which significantly affects downstream tasks. Although speech recognition models provide confidence scores, their accuracy is often hindered by out-of-vocabulary words, mispronunciations, and poor audio quality, leading to uncertain transcriptions. To mitigate these issues, we propose refining the uncertainty quantification of automatic speech recognition (ASR) by leveraging the statistical distribution of recognition uncertainties. To this end, we introduce the concept of dialogue state monitoring as a downstream task to improve with ASR uncertainty modeling. By treating the ASR output as a sample from a language model, we generate a word confusion network (WCN) to represent the recognition uncertainty distribution. We then develop a dialogue state monitoring model that samples from the WCN to match the uncertainty distribution with the actual dialogue states. Experimental results on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset demonstrate that our proposed models outperform conventional ASR confidence scores in dialogue state monitoring tasks. Moreover, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach by integrating it with a slot tagging model, leading to enhanced performance on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset. Our method is further validated through ablation studies, highlighting the contributions of different components. The proposed model is expected to benefit downstream tasks by providing a more accurate understanding of ASR uncertainty, thereby enhancing the overall performance of dialogue systems. The unique characteristics of palm tree modes (PTMs) observed in edge plasma of the JET tokamak remain poorly understood after their initial discovery in 2018. This analysis aims to provide a comprehensive review of the development and core aspects of PTMs found in JET experiments. PTMs are identified by distinctive magnetic fluctuations in the edge plasma, characterized by unique patterns of magnetic field changes and their spatial distribution. Their features vary depending on the discharge parameters and can be classified into four main types based on their frequency and location. PTMs have been linked to enhanced edge radial electron current, increased turbulence, and reduced edge plasma density, often occurring during the late phases of JET's ELMy H-mode scenario. This study also explores the potential connections between PTMs and other edge plasma features, including edge turbulence, soliton-like structures, and associated changes in the edge plasma, with a view to understanding their underlying causes. While the exact causes of PTMs remain unclear, this review provides a thorough examination of the available evidence and suggests avenues for further investigation. Given the complexity of edge plasma behavior, further research is needed to clarify the development and implications of PTMs observed in JET experiments. Hate speech within social media is a pressing issue, encompassing not only text-based insults but also visual and auditory offenses. Existing hate speech identification models are predominantly text-based, often relying on machine learning techniques that analyze textual features. However, these models are susceptible to variations in linguistic and cultural contexts, hindering their performance outside of specific data sets. Furthermore, the methods used to train these models are shrouded in secrecy, making it impossible to gauge their reliability. To address these limitations, we propose a novel, text-to-image generation technique based on the MaLM-Art model, which produces hate speech-related images. We then develop and present a new understandingable hate speech identification model that integrates text and image modalities. This approach involves training a neural network to analyze the connections between text, image, and their combined sample, effectively mitigating the biases in individual modalities. We test our approach using data from the 2021 Hate Speech Identification track of the ODSC Europe 2021 competition, achieving superior results and demonstrating improved generalizability in cross-domain scenarios. Additionally, the proposed method allows for the visualization of the learned features through t-SNE analysis, while making the underlying training data and model architecture fully transparent. We further demonstrate the cross-modal generalization capabilities of our approach by training the model on social media hate speech data from German and evaluating it on Russian hate speech data, achieving a high F1 score of 0.755. We also conduct a thorough feature analysis across multiple data sets and discover that the learned features are consistent in terms of their semantic meaning. This breakthrough in hate speech identification through text-to-image synthesis opens up new avenues for multi-modal learning and understanding in NLP. We believe that the proposed approach can be adapted and applied to a wide range of natural language processing challenges, ultimately contributing to the advancement of NLP. The code and trained models for this research are publicly available at https://github.com/sohsoh/odsc2021-mmlhs. We also invite the community to engage with our research through https://hate-speech-odsc.net. In large-scale wireless communication systems with numerous terminals, effectively managing the complex interactions among terminals is a major challenge. To address this issue, recent research has focused on using artificial intelligence from a system-wide perspective. This paper proposes a novel AI-based framework for wireless transmission systems, enabling individual terminals to make data-driven decisions and reduce computational burdens on the entire system. By formulating a decentralized optimization problem and applying Graph Neural Networks, we derive a stable algorithm for stability and Q-learning. Theoretical analysis and simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves nearly optimal system-wide performance without requiring global data access. Furthermore, the results show that each terminal's performance approaches optimal performance as the number of terminals increases. This approach has the potential to inspire new decentralized AI applications within wireless transmission systems. The code for this paper can be found at \url{https://github.com/Chen-chen-Lin/Decentralized-Reasoning}.

The elevated murder rates in Brazil pose a significant problem, with the state of Goias in Central Brazil being no exception to this issue.  To better understand the context, this research examined the spatial patterns of murders in Goias between 2002 and 2014, using data from the Brazilian Ministry of Justice's National System for Social Information.  By applying the Local Moran's I and cluster analysis methods, this study identified and verified areas with high or low murder rates, and explored the potential causes behind these patterns.  It was found that Goias' murder hotspots were primarily influenced by three factors: (1) urbanization, (2) socio-economic conditions, and (3) the presence of violent organized crime groups.  Furthermore, this research found that the murder clusters in Goias were relatively stable, with some existing for the entire duration of the study and others emerging in the latter half, particularly between 2008-2014.  In terms of geographical distribution, the murder clusters were found to be concentrated in the state's capital city, particularly in areas with higher levels of socio-economic inequality and urbanization.  By exploring the temporal patterns of the murder clusters, this research found that the most significant changes occurred between 2008-2014, with the formation of new clusters during this period.  Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the spatial patterns of murders in Goias and contributes to a deeper understanding of the underlying causes of violence in the region.  It is hoped that this research can inform and assist law enforcement agencies and policymakers in developing effective strategies to combat the high murder rates in Goias.  Finally, this study concludes by discussing its implications and suggesting potential avenues for future research on this topic.  Specifically, this research highlights the need for more effective law enforcement in areas with high levels of organized crime activity, and the importance of addressing socio-economic inequality and promoting urban development in areas with high murder rates.  Additionally, this study suggests that policymakers could explore alternative approaches to law enforcement, such as community-based initiatives and restorative justice programs, in order to address the root causes of violence in Goias.  Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the complex social dynamics underlying the high murder rates in Goias.  By shedding light on these dynamics, this research hopes to inspire policymakers and law enforcement agencies to develop more effective solutions to this problem.  It is through this research that we can work towards creating a safer and more just society for all the people of Goias.

Deep learning model compression through knowledge distillation has gained significant attention. Conventional distillation methods, however, often compromise data flow to achieve model compression, resulting in performance degradation. This paper introduces a new distillation technique called InDistill that preserves data flow during model compression, thereby ensuring the compressed model's accuracy remains intact. InDistill leverages an intermediate feature matching objective to align the features of the teacher and student models, preserving data flow. Additionally, InDistill incorporates a classification loss to refine the student model's outputs, enhancing its accuracy. Experimental results on various tasks and model configurations validate the efficacy of InDistill, with notable improvements in accuracy for models with identical data flows. Notably, InDistill achieves a superior average AUC improvement of 2.8% when compared to the distillation loss alone, with a compression ratio of 8-10. The project's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharakeh/indistill. The pre-trained models are hosted on HuggingFace Model Hub at https://huggingface.co/datasets/indistill-projects. This project has been peer-reviewed.

The well-known $\epsilon$-approximation problem in the streaming model involves creating an accurate estimate of a real function's value based on a single pass through noisy input data. Researchers have developed a robust linear sketch called CountSketch to solve this problem even when faced with malicious noise. However, a recent finding demonstrated that even small amounts of adaptability in the input data can significantly compromise the accuracy of CountSketch sketches. This paper aims to investigate the resilience of CountSketch and related sketches in the presence of adaptable inputs. Specifically, it introduces a new model of adaptability and provides a tight bound on the required number of samples needed to accurately estimate an $\epsilon$-approximation function using these sketches. Furthermore, a new set of non-adaptive inputs, known as "block-adaptive," is introduced, and a precise lower bound on the required samples is established for the specialized sketch of Andoni and Páter. This study's findings have significant implications for the development of robust sketches in the post-adaptive setting, and it raises new questions about the limitations of current sketches in the face of adaptability. In linguistic systems, consistency is crucial for effective communication. We examine if a dynamic labeling system, governed by the principle of similarity, can achieve this consistency. Three key factors influence the labeling process: the perception of similarity, categorization, and preference, which can be manipulated to represent different cognitive models. Our study focuses on the labeling system's ability to evolve and consistency, while also exploring the characteristics of the agents involved. As the number of agents grows, we observe that the dynamic system converges towards a consistent state, but at a slower rate than expected. Furthermore, we identify a critical point where the system's behavior changes from convergence to divergence, and show that certain types of cognitive models can lead to unstable outcomes. To understand the source of this instability, we investigate the labeling process and reveal that agents' preferences play a key role, leading to a significant shift in the understanding of the underlying concept. Our research provides a framework for studying linguistic consistency and can be applied to real-world scenarios, such as crowdsourcing platforms, to improve communication among diverse groups. only provided accurate predictions at the training points, but when momentum was added,

accurate predictions outside the training area, indicating momentum significantly

Blind image restoration, covering problems like blind deblurring and blind denoising, aims to recover a clear image from a degraded observation without knowing its original form. Common approaches assume a degraded observation by convolution with a blur kernel, distorted by noise. To improve the accuracy of restoration results, this research develops an advanced model that represents the distribution of blur kernels as a mixture of Gaussian functions in the frequency domain. The locations of these Gaussian functions and the corresponding weights are learned during the training process, while the scale parameters are determined by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Evaluations play a crucial role in recommending items effectively. To address this challenge, this paper introduces the task of evaluation-based item recommendation. We find that existing methods are inadequate because they ignore the significance of evaluation content in recommending items. To address this shortcoming, we propose the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN). SIFN consists of two interconnected components: a Universal Sentence Encoder that captures item-drivers from reviews and evaluations, and an Interactive Fusion Module that combines review and evaluation information with item features to recommend them. Experimental results on four real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of SIFN over baseline methods. Notably, SIFN outperforms state-of-the-art models by 10.3% AUC and 8.5% NDCG in average metrics on these datasets. We introduce Contrastive Education with Physics-informed Visualization (CEPV), a novel approach to training neural networks using single-shot data, exemplified by identifying substances in water samples. CEPV employs two contrasting methods - positive and negative visualization techniques - to derive dual learning signals. Positive visualization involves training the network to generate images of a specific substance under normal conditions, while negative visualization involves introducing random disturbances to create diverse negative examples for the network to distinguish. By combining these techniques, CEPV produces an enhanced classification layer that, when activated, produces a class probability map, facilitating identification of substances in water samples, even when only a portion is visible. Furthermore, CEPV allows for object detection and classification in cluttered scenes. Experimental results demonstrate CEPV's superiority over competing methods and its ability to successfully apply to diverse scenarios, such as identifying substances in water samples, detecting and classifying objects in traffic scenes, and identifying unknown materials under various lighting conditions. As machine learning models increasingly underpin decision-making processes in sensitive domains, ensuring that these algorithms can be understood by humans assumes greater importance. Interpretability, a multifaceted concept, is still poorly defined, and existing measures focus primarily on detectability rather than learnability. This paper proposes a new, trainable definition of interpretability rooted in human learning, and a associated metric, the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS). CCS quantifies the difficulty of learning an algorithm by measuring the complexity of the information needed to learn it, and the resources required to master that information. We demonstrate the CCS's utility in assessing the learnability of several neural network-based black-box algorithms, and show that it can capture nuances missed by existing, more superficial measures. By offering a trainable perspective on interpretability, our framework offers a more effective way to evaluate and improve algorithmic learnability. We anticipate that this research will inform the development of more transparent and understandable machine learning models. By applying ICP I and II, we create detailed 12 Spitzer/IRAC layer mosaics from Hi-GAL frequencies and corresponding spectral models. ICP II generates 20 component models, with 8 common to all mosaics and 12 others varying depending on the type of sources being analyzed. Our results show 8 broad spectral components, with 5 related to dust and 3 to 2 components for H2O and 2 for CO. Due to limitations in the Hi-GAL data, we couldn't accurately analyze the molecular line component using ICP II. However, we were able to successfully apply ICP I to the entire dataset and use the resulting information to analyze 20,000 sources across the galaxy. Our analysis shows 7 broad spectral components, with 5 related to dust and 2 to 1 H2O and 1 CO component. Our findings also show that ICP II provides more accurate information, but it requires more data and complex frequencies. Our study of 20,000 sources across the galaxy using ICP I reveals 4 main types of sources, with 1,500 star forming sources, 1,500 red supergiant stars, 13,000 dense star forming cores, and 4,000 active star forming regions. Our analysis of the sources' physical properties shows that they vary based on their distance and galactic plane position. Our study also shows that the sources' SEDs are stable over time and that the ICP method is a reliable tool for analyzing the physical properties of the sources. In magnetic resonance imaging, the L-value represents the number of readings taken from a given pixel, ranging from 0 to 255. L-values are typically encoded in a 9-bit Gray code. However, these L-values can provide valuable insights if analyzed individually. To unlock their potential, a deep learning model is proposed that uses the L-values to create enhanced features, leading to improved diagnostic accuracy. To streamline the analysis, a quantized L-value approach is suggested, reducing the number of unique L-values from 255 to 32 through a quantization loss function. This allows the model to focus on the most informative aspects of the imaging data, significantly reducing training time and improving convergence. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach leads to enhanced diagnostic accuracy, outperforming traditional spatial-based methods in breast tissue classification and matching the performance of traditional sequential methods, while also showcasing its ability to achieve state-of-the-art results when used in conjunction with sequential methods for the classification of mammography patterns. Our findings indicate that the proposed approach is versatile and can be applied to a range of computer vision tasks. Crowdsourced labeling is a widely used technique for training machine learning models, but it comes with its own set of issues stemming from noisy and inconsistent data. This research delves into the statistical distributions of crowdsourced labels, proposing a method to measure uncertainty based on entropy and a novel representation of annotator trust known as Human Softmax. This Human Softmax representation is applied across various labeling scenarios, including multi-choice and categorization tasks. Subsequently, an ensemble modeling approach is developed to address classification tasks, which is capable of handling noisy data. Ensemble models are trained on a spectrum of datasets, each with varying levels of noise, which are generated from the Human Softmax distribution. Notably, this method does not rely on data resubmission or post-processing, making it practical for real-world applications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in classifying data with noisy labels, and it even outperforms traditional methods when the noise level is low. Furthermore, this method's ability to estimate noise levels is also evaluated, revealing correlations between these estimates and the method's performance. These findings are consistent across multiple labeling tasks. Finally, this research applies the proposed method to a real-world image classification task, utilizing data collected through crowdsourcing for training an ensemble model, which in turn achieves a high accuracy rate in classifying images. Overall, this research provides a framework for addressing noisy data in machine learning and offers a set of tools for crowdsourced data collection. Subsequently, these tools can be utilized to refine the data collection process and enhance the quality of the data. Ultimately, this research aims to improve the effectiveness of crowdsourced data by addressing its underlying issues. A common approach involves using a source domain with labeled data, but this becomes impractical when there are many unbalanced datasets. This novel technique is called the Domain-informed Neural Network, or DNN, and it is specifically designed to work with a simple yet effective data structure known as the octree. By using a unique representation of the octree, the neural network can efficiently incorporate more information about the environment and make more accurate predictions. Neural radiance fields (NeRF) generate high-quality images of novel views by modeling scene geometry and materials using continuous functions, but current methods are limited to small objects and require precise correspondences between images. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new method, brightness field neural rendering (BF-NeRF), which uses a simplified and efficient function that computes the average material color of a given position, replacing the original volumetric integration process. This simplified function enables the use of lightweight models, smaller memory footprints, and faster inference times, while maintaining the ability to generate high-quality images of large and complex scenes. Furthermore, BF-NeRF can be trained without relying on traditional correspondences, utilizing a novel approach that combines multi-view constraints to recover the material colors of scenes. Our experiments demonstrate that BF-NeRF achieves state-of-the-art performance in both small and large-scale scenes, outperforming existing methods by an order of magnitude in terms of inference speed. Additionally, BF-NeRF's simplified design allows it to accurately render scenes with moving objects and occlusions. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alekseiz/bf-nerf. Current state-of-the-art action detection models heavily rely on strong and precise annotations. However, manually labeling each action instance in every video is impractical due to the massive video library available online. To overcome this limitation, we propose a framework called Spot, which identifies crucial frames containing key actions and applies graph convolutions to infer action relationships based on semantic context. Spot's frame selection process prioritizes salient information and, along with the graph structure, effectively captures complex action dependencies. By integrating spotting and graph inference, we achieve accurate action detection, outperforming existing approaches with minimal reliance on bounding box annotations. Our evaluation on various datasets, including JHMDB, UCF101, Human3D, and ActivityNet, demonstrates the efficacy of Spot in action detection, especially when paired with diverse self-supervised learning loss functions. The code and models are available on our website: \url{https://yuanjieliang.github.io/Spot}. On average, Spot achieves an mAP of 43.4%, surpassing recent action detection models by a margin of 10-20%. Notably, Spot's performance is particularly impressive when evaluated on ActivityNet, achieving an mAP of 24.6%, a significant improvement of over 10% compared to the current best action detection method. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that spotting alone can achieve an mAP of 36.8%, outperforming state-of-the-art action detection models by a substantial margin of over 10%. This suggests that current action detection approaches heavily underestimate the importance of key frames. By leveraging self-supervised learning, we enhance the model's ability to rely on these crucial frames, thereby improving action detection performance. Our proposed graph convolutional structure also contributes to capturing complex action dependencies, particularly when combined with self-supervised learning. Overall, Spot's performance is comparable to that of state-of-the-art action recognition models, demonstrating the model's potential for weakly-guided action detection. Given the extensive evaluation on multiple datasets, we believe that spot has the potential to revolutionize action detection by addressing the limitation of strong annotations. The code and models are available on our website: \url{https://yuanjieliang.github.io/Spot}. On our website, we also provide a visual demonstration of Spot's performance on real-world videos, showcasing the model's ability to effectively detect actions. By leveraging spot, we are able to identify actions that are not explicitly stated in the video title or description, highlighting the model's ability to effectively capture complex action dependencies.

The growing need for enhanced online learning security through data protection has led to the development of Federated Learning. This method trains a model without revealing sensitive student data to the server or instructor. Despite its potential, existing FL implementations often rely on a server, which can compromise student privacy. This paper proposes a new server-free, multi-client Federated Learning model, DP-REC, that enables secure model training using protected learning records. DP-REC employs secure token matching and distributed token generation to verify data authenticity, while using differential privacy for data protection. DP-REC maintains data confidentiality by encrypting model updates and storing encrypted data in tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that DP-REC reduces communication overhead by 90%, achieves 85% of the accuracy of traditional models, and protects student data effectively while using differential privacy. This innovation aims to improve the privacy and security of online educational platforms. DP-REC's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenXinyu95/DPRec. Remote-controlled vehicles like telepresence robots have gained popularity in various fields such as agriculture, environmental monitoring, and search and rescue operations. To make these vehicles user-friendly, a straightforward and intuitive control interface is essential. This study focuses on evaluating the quality of experience (QoE) for controlling telepresence robots using a straightforward interface on a tablet. Twenty participants remotely controlled a quadrotor drone to complete tasks while experiencing the tablet interface under different conditions that mimicked real-world wireless remote control and evaluating their performance. The results showed that users preferred the original interface over a simplified one in terms of remote control speed and accuracy, as measured by a subjective quality test. The data also revealed that users who experienced the original interface performed better than those who experienced the simplified interface, indicating that a balance between usability and functionality is crucial for an effective remote control system. This study provides insights into designing user-friendly interfaces for remote-controlled systems. The data and analysis tools are publicly available on https://github.com/usc-iris/QoE_telepresence.git. The application is also available as a standalone service at https://bayesilm-forecasting.herokuapp.com. Our findings highlight the importance of computational considerations in machine learning and suggest that overparameterization may be an effective strategy for tackling problems that are difficult to solve with basic models.  Our theoretical results are supported by experiments using artificial neural networks.  Our research also reveals that successful generalization through sparsity requires the number of computations needed to evaluate a loss function to grow at least as quickly as a polynomial function for certain data distributions, and that this lower bound can be tightened further for Gaussian mixture models.  Our experiments using artificial neural networks confirm these findings and demonstrate that the degree of sparsity in successful models can be reduced by limiting the computational resources available to the model.  Our research also shows that the success of overparameterization in practice is not solely due to computational limitations, as it can also be attributed to the use of loss functions that are not consistent with the data.  Our experiments using artificial neural networks confirm these findings and demonstrate that the success of overparameterization can be replicated using basic models, such as linear regression, under controlled conditions. Researchers have successfully observed for the first time in history the transfer of both transverse and longitudinal beam emittances during a particle beam interaction. This groundbreaking experiment involved directing a low-energy electron beam at a stationary nickel foil, using the NSF's Heavy Ion Accelerator at Iowa State University. The resulting beam properties were then measured at an energy of 10 keV. The findings confirmed that emittance transfer follows the expected patterns of both ablation and ionization processes, exhibiting distinct characteristics for each phenomenon. Notably, the total transverse emittance showed greater values in the ionization process, whereas the total longitudinal emittance showed greater values in the ablation process. The experimental results were also validated by comparing them to simulations based on the EPICS software system, which provided a good match. The successful outcome of this experiment opens the door for future research on emittance transfer in particle accelerator applications, particularly those involving beam-plasma interactions. This research may have significant implications for future experiments, such as plasma-based accelerators and beam-induced sputtering studies. Predicting the future paths of multiple moving objects in a given scene is essential for various real-world applications such as autonomous driving and surveillance. To accurately forecast the trajectories of multiple objects, one must consider not only an object's past history but also its interactions with other objects in the scene. However, traditional approaches focusing solely on individual histories often neglect these interactions, resulting in inaccuracies. To address this, recent socially-aware trajectory forecasting methods incorporate both individual and social context. However, these methods typically assume a fixed understanding of how objects interact, which may lead to subpar performance when interactions change over time. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a new approach that combines a self-supervised module with a socially-aware variational autoencoder. The self-supervised module updates an object's past history to reflect its current social context, while the socially-aware variational autoencoder generates multiple possible trajectory possibilities, taking into account both individual and social factors. By reevaluating and reforecasting the trajectories when social factors change, this approach significantly improves forecasting accuracy. Our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on publicly available datasets. Notably, this approach achieves a relative improvement of 24.5% in NDE, 26.8% inADE, when compared to the top-performing method on the Argoverse motion forecasting challenge leaderboard. In the field of digital pathology, experts use image analysis to identify and classify blood components in tissue samples. To achieve this, researchers employed ensemble learning methods with multiple convolutional neural networks. The networks, trained on blood-rich images from a lymph node dataset, were combined to improve the accuracy of identification and classification tasks. An ensemble approach was applied using two aggregation techniques - weighted averaging and voting processes. The ensemble models were found to outperform individual component networks in various tasks, specifically in localizing and categorizing vessels, cells, and blood plasma. An analysis of the model components revealed that distinct networks emphasize different aspects of blood objects, such as vessel boundaries, cell shapes, and plasma environments. Upon manual evaluation, it was determined that the combination of networks brings about a 10% reduction in error compared to individual component networks, primarily through a 50% decrease in false positive rates in identifying blood plasma. The ensemble models, consisting of a network aggregation process, demonstrate the potential to outperform standalone deep learning models in terms of localization and categorization accuracy. The proposed models can be utilized in a clinical setting to support the analysis of lymph node datasets for diagnostic and research purposes. We introduce a free, open-source software platform called pyStoNED, designed to
compute the optimal solutions of several popular multi-objective programming
problems in economics, including the StoNED model, using a revised version of
the non-differentiable convex multi-objective programming algorithm originally
developed by Laestandes and Mavrot. In addition to this algorithm, our
platform employs another variant that we had previously introduced to maintain
the original properties of multi-objective programming, including the creation
of efficient Pareto-frontier sets and the calculation of step-wise solutions.

can be easily utilized in both the R and Python programming languages. We provide
a comprehensive example of using pyStoNED to analyze the European investment
efficiency data set. The software, its documentation, and associated examples
are publicly available at https://github.com/mbreuer/pyStoNED. A corresponding
R-package, called RpyStoNED, is also available at https://github.com/mbreuer/RpyStoNED.

Ultimately, our analysis reveals that the Kaldi system produces more accurate results, albeit at a slower processing speed. In contrast, the Pytorch system offers faster processing times but slightly inferior performance. In addition to presenting our findings, we are also releasing the diarization code and annotated data for the German language to facilitate further research and development. Transformers' sequential dependence on non-exchangeable assumptions has hindered deep learning's potential for parallelization, but recent research suggests a new approach with vitals-like attention and non-commutative product could circumvent this limitation. This has led to novel architectures such as NFT, which demonstrates faster convergence and higher accuracy on small datasets like CIFAR10, but struggles with scalability. To address this issue, we propose a new method, non-exchangeable tangent core kernel (NFT-K), which combines the benefits of NFT with data parallelization using a vits-like attention mechanism. By integrating a Gaussian noise layer with a tangent kernel, NFT-K achieves state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet while being resistant to adversarial attacks and having robust generalization properties. Our empirical results show that NFT-K outperforms existing models on ImageNet, with a superior performance on tasks like out-of-distribution image denoising, image classification, and adversarial robustness. Additionally, NFT-K's ability to parallelize its training and inference processes enables it to achieve a 5x speedup compared to other models. This paper presents a comprehensive empirical study of NFT-K's capabilities and explores its potential applications in computer vision. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/chenyilongpipe/nft-k. Non-Hermitian systems have garnered significant attention for their unique topological characteristics, exceptional features, and potential industrial applications. A particular class of these systems, one-dimensional chiral models without Hermiticity, are especially intriguing due to their robust topological properties and interactive versatility. In this study, we investigate the impact of non-Hermitian strength on one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological models, discovering that as the non-Hermitian strength diminishes to zero, the model's topological features and exceptional points vanish. Conversely, when the non-Hermitian strength approaches infinity, the model loses its topological characteristics, manifesting as band gap closures and reconfigurations, and new zero-mode locations. Our research also reveals that by introducing interactions between fermions, the model's topological features can be manipulated, such as moving topological features from free to interacting systems, and using interactions to control the model's topological characteristics. These findings offer valuable insights into the design and control of one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological models. Furthermore, we propose a method to experimentally realize a bulk-topological phase transition in a Harper-Hofstadter model via an optical lattice and laser interference. Our research contributes to the understanding and manipulation of one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological models, and may lead to novel applications in quantum technologies. Using molecular dynamics simulations, our research examines the relationship between the residual entropy of molecular models and their viscosity. A comprehensive analysis is conducted across a broad spectrum of model potentials, covering pairs with and without volume-exclusion features. Specifically, we evaluate the residual entropy of Stellan models, as well as the viscosity of their pairs, near their critical points. Notably, our results indicate a direct correlation between the remaining entropy and viscosity of fluids, with this connection being more pronounced in pairs of model potentials without volume-exclusion. Furthermore, we find that the residual entropy of these exclusionless pairs serves as an adequate proxy for estimating the residual entropy of their viscous fluid phases. In contrast, for pairs with volume-exclusion, this correlation is found to be less significant. These findings are subsequently extended to a comprehensive set of model-hamiltonian data, enabling us to develop a novel, data-driven parameterization for estimating the residual entropy of fluid phases based on their temperature and density. Overall, our research provides new insights into the relationship between the residual entropy and viscosity of fluids, with important implications for their understanding and characterization. Moreover, our work offers a valuable resource for researchers tackling the challenging task of designing supercritical fluids with optimal transport properties. The invariant-set concept, a superdeterministic idea, suggests that a random variable can't be predicted but its range is limited, leading to nonrandom behavior. To explore this notion, we developed a concealed-variable model creating a two-dimensional random field following the invariant-set principle. Our primary goal was to determine the probability distribution of the field's entropy within this restricted set, using the information-sharing concept as a starting point. However, the calculation proved to be extremely challenging, and we were only able to estimate its value under specific assumptions about its distribution. Additionally, we examined the field's entropy's mean and spread (statistical variance) within the invariant set and found them to be closely linked. Furthermore, we discovered that the spread is directly related to the field's entropy's negative value, indicating superdeterministic behavior. To validate the model's effectiveness, we applied it to a simple scenario involving a concealed-variable model of a binary random variable. Our results show that the statistical variance can serve as an estimator for the underlying field's negative entropy, and we found that the estimated spread closely matches the true value in various Monte Carlo simulations. The findings suggest that the invariant-set concept is a viable superdeterministic idea within the concealed-variable framework. However, the model's simplicity prevents it from being a comprehensive explanation of the Bell Test data, and we propose that incorporating additional concealed variables could potentially address this limitation. Our research also reveals that the statistical variance of a random variable can be an indicator of its underlying negative entropy, and this relationship may be a general phenomenon. Further investigation is required to explore the applicability of this phenomenon to other superdeterministic models. For mixed-criticality embedded systems, ensuring real-time system safety is a top priority. The growing trend in embedded systems is to integrate a hypervisor, as hypervisors play a crucial role in achieving safety by isolating system components. However, existing hypervisors are not well-suited for mixed-criticality embedded systems due to several limitations, primarily because they were designed with primary-optional scheduling in mind, not the reverse. To address this, we have developed T-Visor, a new hypervisor that incorporates virtualization assistance and is built on top of the PREEMPT_RT kernel. T-Visor outperforms current hypervisors by providing efficient isolation, integrating a mixed-criticality scheduler, and leveraging hardware virtualization support. A real-time embedded system testbed was used to evaluate T-Visor's performance, demonstrating its superiority over the Xen hypervisor in terms of isolation, scheduling, and virtualization assistance. The results show that T-Visor can handle context switches up to 5.8 times faster and provide more responsive system responses. To facilitate practical applications, we have also introduced a new mixed-criticality scheduling approach, called TD, which is lightweight and can function without prior knowledge of task priorities. The TD scheduling algorithm was integrated into T-Visor and achieved a 40% reduction in scheduling overhead compared to round-robin scheduling. The proposed TD scheduling approach and T-Visor hypervisor were formally verified using the Coq proof assistant, ensuring their correctness and reliability. A comprehensive evaluation of T-Visor was conducted using the AUTOSAR Benchmark to assess its performance, demonstrating its ability to handle real-time embedded systems efficiently. The results show that T-Visor can provide superior real-time guarantees, achieving a response time within 10 microseconds and a context switch time within 30 microseconds. The evaluation also highlights T-Visor's ability to improve system safety by providing isolation, reducing interference, and enhancing overall system robustness. A significant challenge in computer vision involves creating a comprehensive and high-quality wide-format image from individual snapshots captured at varying heights. Current techniques often struggle to account for changes in perspective when shooting from multiple angles, particularly in scenarios where the camera is not aligned with the gravitational direction. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a simplified method for merging images by leveraging a fundamental property of perspective projection. By assuming that the camera's axis of rotation approximates the gravitational direction, we develop an efficient image-stitching pipeline that: Firstly, generates a high-quality 3D point cloud using depth information; Secondly, estimates the camera's pose in the point cloud's coordinate system; Thirdly, warps individual images onto a unified coordinate system; Lastly, combines the warped images to form a complete and high-quality image. By integrating our novel approach with a state-of-the-art deblurring technique, we demonstrate that our method outperforms existing panoramic stitching algorithms, particularly in scenarios where the camera is not aligned with the gravitational direction. To facilitate practical applications, we also present a straightforward implementation of this technique. Our proposed method has been extensively evaluated using a diverse dataset consisting of over 1,000 images and various ground truths, showcasing its effectiveness in a range of scenarios. Furthermore, we have tested our approach on real-world images and compared it with other state-of-the-art stitching algorithms, both visually and quantitatively. The results reveal that our method produces superior outcomes in a substantial number of cases, underscoring its value for practical image stitching applications. In various fields, researchers study systems that both fluctuate randomly and give rise to organized patterns and structures. Examples include pattern formation in fluid motion, the organization of animal social groups, and crystal growth. This study examines how patterned states persist when subjected to continuous, wide-spectrum noise. We find that in such cases, the patterns that emerge are often rooted in stable, long-lasting data that have inherent symmetries and organization. This data can be thought of as a form of 'blueprint' that endures, in contrast to other variables that are erased by the noise. We demonstrate the significance of this approach by re-examining several noise-driven systems, including Rayleigh-Benard convection, chemical reactions on surfaces, and snowflake growth. In each case, the patterns that endure have a common thread - they can be represented as vector fields that embody key physical principles. This approach provides new insights into the underlying mechanisms governing these systems, and it highlights the importance of heritable data in low-entropy states. We also explore the broader implications of this framework and suggest potential avenues for future research. Ultimately, this study aims to inspire researchers to uncover the enduring blueprints that underlie patterned states in various contexts. A major public health concern persists globally due to intestinal parasites,
despite their relatively small number of species, $257$. In this study, we employed
Deep Belief Networks to accurately classify intestinal parasites, resulting in
high precision rates. Using CBIR, we compared the accuracy of DBN and
Nearest-Neighbor classifiers using features derived from host images and parasite
skins. Our findings demonstrate that DBN outperforms Nearest-Neighbor in skin-only
extracts, while both methods exhibit comparable accuracy when combined with host
features. Notably, when combined with host features, DBN's accuracy surpasses
existing state-of-the-art methods by $20\%$. This research contributes to the
solution of the parasite identification challenge through CBIR. Inspired by this
success, we plan to further enhance intestinal parasite categorization by
integrating DBN with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks. Our future work will
involve extensive data augmentation to train a deep learning model that can
generalize well even with limited labeled data, ultimately enabling CBIR to
categorize intestinal parasites effectively. The data and code used in this

The task of aspect-based sentiment analysis, crucial for understanding how people feel about specific topics, has been complicated by the presence of varying levels of emotion intensity and explicit or implicit emotional markers. To address this issue, we propose a novel pre-trained language model, called LEMAP, which is designed to capture the underlying emotional sentiment by contrasting positive and negative emotional perspectives with objectivity. By incorporating a guided contrastive pre-training method, LEMAP is able to learn emotion-rich representations that are then fine-tuned for aspect-based sentiment analysis, outperforming existing models on benchmark datasets. Notably, our experiments demonstrate that LEMAP achieves improved results when the number of negative labels is reduced, underscoring the model's effectiveness in extracting emotional sentiment. Additionally, an ablation study confirms the efficacy of the guided contrastive pre-training approach, which is further validated by the model's ability to accurately identify emotional markers. The implementation details and the trained LEMAP model are publicly available on GitHub. transparency and control for each party. We've explored this issue in the context
